obscure

ub-SKYOOR — rhymes with 'unsure'; if something is obscure, you're unsure you've ever heard of it. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Obscure is little known; not discovered or familiar to most people.

She loved collecting records by obscure bands that almost no one had heard of.

Example

A poet published a single small book in 1900 and sold about thirty copies. Today her name appears in no textbooks, and only a handful of scholars have ever read her work. Even the library that owns the book misfiled it for decades.

Someone known to almost nobody is obscure. Unlike 'forgotten,' which implies people once knew and then lost track, an obscure figure may never have been widely known at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unknown: Unknown is absolute — nobody recognizes the thing, or nobody even knows it exists. Obscure sits a step short of that: an obscure band or poet is known, but only to a small circle. If a few devoted fans can name it, it is obscure rather than truly unknown.

little-known: Little-known says exactly what it sounds like: recognized by only a few people. Obscure means the same and adds a shade of distance — an obscure fact feels buried, the kind a specialist digs up on purpose. Little-known is the plain measure; obscure hints that you had to hunt.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

famous: known by a great many people

prominent: widely noticed and important

Where it sits · how few people know it — unfamiliar → obscure → unheard-of

unfamiliar vs. obscure: Unfamiliar is weaker than obscure — an unfamiliar name is simply new to you, while an obscure one is unknown to almost everyone.

unheard-of vs. obscure: Unheard-of is stronger than obscure: an obscure writer has at least a few devoted readers, but an unheard-of one has essentially none.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ob-

prefix — ob-: over, against (Latin)

root — -scure

root — -scure: covered, dark (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin obscurus meant 'covered over, dark.' Something covered in darkness can't be seen — and by extension, an obscure person or fact stays hidden from public knowledge.

Use the root in a new word: obscurity

Use the root in a new word: obscurity: The actor faded into obscurity after his only film flopped.
